title: The GenAI Boom Will Lift Supermicro, But It Will Lift Others, Too
gist: Supermicro's June-2026 quarter delivered $11.12 billion in revenue (+93.2%) and record profitability ($1.18 billion net income, 10.6% of sales), with AI systems at $6.69 billion and a single customer — almost certainly SpacexAI's Colossus 2 — at 28% of fiscal 2026 revenue. The author's core point is that the GenAI buildout is not a Supermicro-exclusive trade: Dell will land roughly the same ~$60 billion AI systems business in its fiscal 2027, and both remain hostage to Nvidia's CPU/GPU allocation decisions.

insights.claim: Server OEMs and ODMs are structurally low-profit businesses relative to enterprise software, which extracts two to four times more profit per dollar of customer spending — a permanent ceiling on hardware-vendor multiples even during an AI boom.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Cap valuation expectations for AI-server names: revenue can compound at 80-90% while net margin stays in the single digits, so the trade is volume/absolute-dollar earnings, not margin re-rating.
insights.quote: the enterprise software racket, which for now at least can command maybe two, three, or four times the profits out of a given dollar of spending from customers
insights.locator: It seems like every business, with the exceptions

insights.claim: Supermicro's AI systems business functions more like an ODM (few configurations, huge volume, tech-titan customers) than an OEM, even though it retains a few thousand low-volume enterprise customers and a channel that buys motherboards, cards, enclosures, switches, storage and racks.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: ODM-like concentration means Supermicro's earnings quality is closer to a contract manufacturer's than a diversified enterprise vendor's — watch customer concentration, not customer count.
insights.locator: Supermicro has been bridging the gap between OEM and ODM

insights.claim: Supermicro's de-emphasized subsystems business (motherboards, components) grew 2.4X year on year to $278 million in the June 2026 quarter, showing the component arm is still compounding despite the company barely discussing it.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A hidden, higher-attach component line growing 140%+ is an under-modeled optionality in the Supermicro story.
insights.quote: I think the subsystems business grew by 2.4X in the quarter, to $278 million
insights.locator: This data runs out to the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026

insights.claim: Supermicro posted $11.12 billion in revenue in the June 2026 quarter, up 93.2 percent year on year, with the systems business alone at $10.84 billion, up 92.2 percent.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Near-doubling top line confirms the AI server buildout is still accelerating through mid-2026, not rolling over.
insights.locator: Add it all up, and Supermicro raked in

insights.claim: Supermicro's AI systems revenue reached $6.69 billion in the June quarter, up 64.2 percent year on year and 60 percent of total revenues — meaning AI grew materially slower than the 93 percent total, with non-AI CPU servers doing the incremental lifting.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The AI-vs-total growth divergence is the tell that a product transition, not demand, capped the quarter — a setup for a re-acceleration in coming quarters.
insights.quote: up 64.2 percent year on year and comprising 60 percent of its overall revenues
insights.locator: But, in the fourth quarter, as Supermicro's sales of AI systems

insights.claim: Operating income rose 6.6X to $1.49 billion and net income rose 6X to $1.18 billion in the June quarter — 10.6 percent of revenues, the highest net-income-to-revenue ratio in Supermicro's history and by far the largest absolute quarterly profit.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Operating leverage on rackscale/rowscale systems is finally showing up; the 10.6% net margin is the number to benchmark future quarters against.
insights.quote: this is by far the most profitable the company has ever been in one quarter in an absolute dollars sense
insights.locator: Add it all up, and Supermicro raked in

insights.claim: The June quarter was not Supermicro's revenue peak — Q2 fiscal 2026 posted $12.68 billion — so sequential revenue actually declined even as profitability hit a record.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Sequential revenue decline with rising margin argues mix/pricing improvement rather than demand loss; headline-only readers may misprice the print.
insights.locator: This is not the highest revenue Supermicro has ever had

insights.claim: Supermicro ended the June quarter with $7.52 billion in cash, of which $1.4 billion came from new common stock sales and $4.2 billion from convertible preferred shares — the balance sheet was built by dilution and converts, not operating cash.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: $5.6 billion of the $7.52 billion cash pile is externally raised — model share count and conversion overhang, and note the working-capital intensity that forced the raise.
insights.quote: with $1.4 billion coming from sales of new common stock to Wall Street and $4.2 billion coming from convertible preferred shares
insights.locator: Supermicro ended the quarter with $7.52 billion in cash

insights.claim: For all of fiscal 2026 Supermicro booked $39.06 billion in sales (+77.8%), $2.77 billion operating income (2.2X) and $2.23 billion net income (2.1X, 5.5% of revenues).
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A 5.5% full-year net margin against a 10.6% exit quarter frames how much margin expansion is already banked going into fiscal 2027.
insights.locator: For all of fiscal 2026, Supermicro brought in $39.06 billion

insights.claim: The handoff from Nvidia's Grace-Blackwell rackscale systems to the Vera-Rubin generation opened a revenue gap at Supermicro in the June quarter, a mechanical product-transition air pocket rather than a demand break.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Expect the same air pocket at every Nvidia generational handoff — a repeatable calendar for shorting/buying AI-server names around transitions.
insights.quote: has left a bit of a revenue gap
insights.locator: The fact is, the transition between the Nvidia

insights.claim: Supermicro backfilled the AI air pocket by selling large volumes of conventional servers to its biggest customers, who are consolidating non-AI workloads onto fewer, more efficient machines specifically to free datacenter space and power for GenAI accelerated systems.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A second-order demand channel: the AI buildout is itself driving a traditional server refresh cycle — bullish for general-purpose CPU server and x86 supply chains, not just GPU boxes.
insights.quote: And it almost filled in that AI systems slowdown.
insights.locator: So this time around, Supermicro sold a ton

insights.claim: The GenAI supercomputer market is as choppy as the old HPC market because budgets are only loosely coupled to product roadmaps and are gated by datacenter space, power, and the customer's ability to prepay for systems that must all converge at the right moment.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Treat quarterly AI-infrastructure prints as lumpy project revenue; power and prepayment availability, not chip supply alone, are the binding constraints to track.
insights.quote: more constrained by the availability of datacenter space, power, and money to prepay for AI systems and have it all come together at precisely the right time
insights.locator: The traditional HPC supercomputer market was always choppy

insights.claim: Supermicro's June-quarter shortfall against its own $11–12.5 billion guidance implies between $100 million and $1.4 billion of AI systems slipped into fiscal 2027, with the author narrowing the real slippage to roughly $600–700 million.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Slipped-not-lost revenue means the September and December quarters carry a built-in catch-up tailwind — the guide-down is mistimed, not a demand miss.
insights.quote: that implies that somewhere between $100 million and $1.4 billion in AI systems got pushed
insights.locator: In fact, some AI system orders that were supposed to land

insights.claim: Supermicro guided Q1 fiscal 2027 to $14.5–15.5 billion, a sequential jump driven partly by early Vera-Rubin ramp but mostly still by Grace-Blackwell systems.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Blackwell-class volume is still the earnings engine into late 2026 — Rubin timing risk is smaller near-term than headlines suggest.
insights.locator: Q1 F2027 is guiding between $14.5 billion

insights.claim: Supermicro guided fiscal 2027 revenue to $65–72 billion, a $68.5 billion midpoint implying roughly 78 percent growth on top of fiscal 2026's 77.8 percent — two consecutive years of near-doubling.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A $68.5 billion company guiding 78% growth is the single most aggressive AI-infrastructure forecast in the OEM/ODM tier; any downward revision is the key risk event.
insights.locator: Looking ahead to fiscal 2027, at the mid-point of guidance

insights.claim: The author models fiscal 2027 operating income at $5.21 billion and net income at $4.18 billion (6.1 percent of revenues), with margin expansion coming from higher Vera-Rubin system prices and Supermicro's improving cost curve on rowscale systems with integrated power and liquid cooling.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A concrete earnings anchor: ~$4.2 billion net income for FY2027 versus $2.23 billion in FY2026 — use it to test whether the stock is pricing in the doubling.
insights.quote: I am pegging operating income at that revenue level for fiscal 2027 at $5.21 billion, and net income will be around $4.18 billion, or 6.1 percent of revenues
insights.locator: Looking ahead to fiscal 2027, at the mid-point of guidance

insights.claim: Because the AI systems business is so lumpy, Supermicro should be evaluated on annual rather than quarterly results — the author explicitly frames quarterly volatility as noise around a multi-year buildout curve running from the fiscal 2010 cloud boom to the current GenAI phase.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Quarterly misses in this cohort are buyable if the annual trajectory is intact; avoid trading the print.
insights.quote: Given how choppy the AI systems business is, I think it is wise to look at Supermicro on an annual basis as much as on a quarterly one.
insights.locator: Given how choppy the AI systems business is

insights.claim: CEO Charles Liang put fiscal Q4 mix at 60–70 percent traditional accelerated (mostly Nvidia GPU) machines, 10–20 percent agentic AI sandboxing or edge AI, and roughly 20 percent traditional servers, storage and IoT.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Agentic-AI sandbox and edge AI is already a 10-20% revenue line — an emerging CPU-heavy category distinct from GPU training that few models break out.
insights.quote: with another other 10 percent to 20 percent being for this agentic AI sandboxing or edge AI
insights.locator: Supermicro founder and chief executive officer Charles Liang said

themes.theme: Manufacturing footprint and rack power density

insights.claim: Supermicro can build more than 3,000 direct-liquid-cooling racks a month at up to 240 kilowatts each, plus 3,000 air-cooled racks a month, and is now designing and prototyping 500 kilowatt racks.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A jump from 240kW to 500kW racks doubles per-rack power draw — read straight through to grid, transformer, busway and liquid-cooling suppliers as the next bottleneck.
insights.quote: it can produce more than 3,000 direct liquid cooling racks a month (up to 240 kilowatts per rack) and 3,000 air-cooled racks per month; 500 kilowatt racks are being designed and prototyped now
insights.locator: Right now, it can produce more than 3,000

insights.claim: Supermicro now holds nearly 4 million square feet of design and factory space in the United States alone, plus substantial factories in Taiwan, Malaysia and the Netherlands, and has just opened a Silicon Valley rowscale facility focused on optical networking and datacenter-scale systems.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: US-heavy manufacturing is a tariff and onshoring hedge; the optical networking push signals where the next attach-rate margin comes from.
insights.quote: Supermicro has just opened up a new rowscale computing facility in Silicon Valley to work on optical networking and datacenter-scale systems
insights.locator: Supermicro has just opened up a new rowscale computing facility

insights.claim: A single customer accounted for 28 percent of Supermicro's fiscal 2026 revenue — roughly $11 billion — which the author identifies as almost certainly SpacexAI and its Colossus 2 supercomputer.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: 28% single-customer concentration is the largest hidden risk in the Supermicro story — any pause in Colossus 2 capex reprices the equity instantly.
insights.quote: Interestingly Supermicro had one customer who alone accounted for 28 percent of revenues in fiscal 2026.
insights.locator: Interestingly Supermicro had one customer

insights.claim: Colossus 2 capacity is mostly rented by Google and Anthropic at an estimated $920 million and $1.25 billion per month respectively — implying roughly $26 billion a year of AI compute rental flowing from two model builders into one neocloud.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Hyperscaler-to-neocloud rental at $2+ billion a month is the cash flow underwriting the whole server order book; monitor those contracts as the leading indicator for the entire AI hardware chain.
insights.quote: This is almost certainly SpacexAI, with the Colossus 2 supercomputer, which is mostly being rented by Google and Anthropic, for an estimated $920 million and $1.25 billion per month, respectively.
insights.locator: This is almost certainly SpacexAI

insights.claim: Nine customers each spent over $1 billion with Supermicro in fiscal 2026 and together made up about half of its revenue — CoreWeave plus seven others alongside the 28 percent whale.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Half of a $39 billion revenue base sits with nine buyers — the AI server market is a handful of counterparties, so credit and capex discipline at neoclouds is the systemic risk.
insights.quote: Supermicro also said that it had nine customers who spent over $1 billion. So that is CoreWeave and seven other companies.
insights.locator: Supermicro also said that it had nine customers

themes.theme: Dell parity and the Nvidia allocation chokepoint

insights.claim: Dell will book roughly $60 billion in AI system sales in its fiscal 2027 ending January and perhaps $120 billion in total datacenter sales — meaning Dell and Supermicro will run AI systems businesses of about the same size, around $60 billion each.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: The GenAI server trade is not a Supermicro monopoly; Dell captures equal AI dollars on a far larger, more diversified base — a relative-value argument for Dell over the pure play.
insights.quote: But Dell and Supermicro will have about the same sized AI systems businesses, at around $60 billion each.
insights.locator: The thing is, as fast as Supermicro expects to grow

insights.claim: Dell's enterprise customer base numbers in the millions of companies worldwide, versus Supermicro's few thousand direct customers plus channel — a distribution moat Supermicro cannot replicate even at matched AI revenue.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: When AI capex normalizes, Dell's enterprise long tail cushions the fall while Supermicro's concentrated hyperscaler book does not.
insights.locator: The thing is, as fast as Supermicro expects to grow

insights.claim: The determinant of who wins AI system revenue is CPU and GPU allocation, which is controlled by the chip supplier rather than the system builders — making Supermicro's and Dell's growth a function of Nvidia's allocation decisions, not their own execution.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Value accrues to the allocator: system builders are price-takers on supply, so the durable margin sits at Nvidia, and OEM/ODM share shifts are a policy variable set upstream.
insights.quote: It all comes down to CPU and GPU allocations, and we all know who controls them.
insights.locator: It all comes down to CPU and GPU allocations
